items.summary: Welcome to the 26th edition of Cloudflare's DDoS Threat Report. This edition covers the third quarter of 2026 — July, August, and September — and returns the series to its quarterly cadence following the combined H1 2026 volume. The analysis is produced by Cloudforce One , Cloudflare's Threat Intelligence organization, providing a comprehensive analysis of the evolving threat landscape of Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks based on data from the Cloudflare network . Key insights Short-burst, low-bandwidth attacks lasting under 10 minutes and 1 Gbps surged by 208%. Conversely, hyper-volumetric attacks exceeding 1 Tbps plummeted by nearly 69% from Q2, possibly a reflection of law enforcement actions against four major Internet of Things (IoT) botnets earlier in the year. However, variants continue to emerge, proving that IoT botnets remain a durable, high-volume threat to network infrastructure. Threat actors dramatically shifted their reflection and amplification tactics, abruptly abandoning CLDAP floods, which collapsed by 99.5% quarter-over-quarter. Instead, attackers pivoted heavily toward other connectionless protocols, driving a 215% surge in DNS amplification and a 122% increase in general UDP floods. Attack targets broadened significantly across both industries and geographies, with the United States reclaiming the most-attacked position from China. Canada and Israel experienced sharp spikes in targeted attacks — jumping 10 and 7 spots respectively — while juggling geopolitical tensions, trade disputes, and contentious domestic events. At the same time, the operational focus shifted away from media organizations toward a wider array of industry targets, including consumer services, Internet infrastructure, and adult entertainment. Q3 by the numbers: 8,200 DDoS attacks every hour Across its network in the third quarter of 2026, Cloudflare autonomously mitigated 18.2 million network-layer DDoS attacks and 14.4 trillion HTTP DDoS requests. That works out to approximately 8,226 network-layer DDoS attacks per hour, or about 197,400 per day — one attack every 0.44 seconds. The quarter's mitigated traffic totaled 272.6 PB at the network layer and 95.1 PB at the HTTP layer. More swarms, fewer giants Short-burst, mid-range, high-count attacks — the operational signature of DDoS-for-hire "booter" services — accelerated this quarter. These attacks primarily targeted computer software, gambling and casinos, and information technology industries. Cloudflare autonomously mitigated 18.2 million network-layer DDoS attacks in Q3 2026, a +208% increase from the same quarter in 2025 : 96% ended in under 10 minutes 98% stayed under 1 Gbps, more than enough to overwhelm a server or website On the other hand, network-level hyper-volumetric attacks (those exceeding 1 Tbps) reversed course, dropping to 251 attacks in Q3 from 805 in Q2 — coinciding with law enforcement action in early 2026 that dismantled four of the largest IoT DDoS botnets: Aisuru, KimWolf, JackSkid, and Mossad. Still, IoT-based botnets remain a durable high-volume threat as the ecosystem churns through new variants such as Dysphoria and Evooo1Bot . Mirai -classified mitigation peaked in August at 57.23 PB, representing 46.5% of all mitigated network-layer bytes in Q3, including four days — August 16, 19, 23, and 25 — that each cleared three petabytes. The quarter's longest sustained Mirai attack ran 49.7 hours between August 19 and August 21. Vector shifts: the collapse of CLDAP and rise of UDP The most dramatic vector shift of the quarter was downward. CLDAP (Connectionless Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) attacks — where small queries with a forged victim IP address trick public domain controllers (UDP 389) into reflecting massive, amplified responses back at the target — experienced a dramatic +580% quarter-over-quarter surge in the first half of the year before collapsing to just 0.05% of attacks in Q3. Meanwhile, DNS amplification surged 215% to account for 3.43% of all network-layer attacks, exploiting open DNS resolvers in a similar reflection-and-amplification pattern to CLDAP: small spoofed queries, large replies directed at the victim. Other UDP floods climbed from 14.06% to 31.31% of network-layer attacks. UDP is a connectionless transport protocol, which makes it a convenient vehicle for raw volumetric attacks: attackers send large numbers of UDP packets to random or specific ports on the target, forcing the target to check for a listening application and respond, consuming its network and compute resources. Most-attacked industry While Media, Production & Publishing remained the most-attacked industry in Q3 2026, its overall share is roughly a quarter of its Q2 level, and the focus has moved across a wider set of industries. Internet rose from outside the top 10 to #6; Consumer Services and Adult Entertainment also climbed in, reaching #8 and #9 respectively. Most-attacked locations Geographic surges: Canada and Israel climb the ranks Adding to an already turbulent period of bilateral trade disputes, Canada jumped from #16 to #6, driven by attacks against its Retail, Telecommunications, Service providers & carriers, and Marketing & advertising industries. Israel moved 7 spots to take #10 as a result of sustained DDoS activity in mid-September. While this period was marked by contentious decisions ahead of parliamentary elections and the Rosh Hashanah holiday, there was also a massive, documented surge in hostile cyber warfare targeting Israel this year. Top 10 The United States was the most-attacked location in Q3 2026, while China was number #2 and Indonesia rose into the top three at 2.93% of total attacks. The U.S.-China pairing at the top is consistent with the first half of 2026, when China finished #1 and the U.S. #2; the countries have traded positions as attention and attacker preferences shift. Strengthening global defenses and helping to defend the Internet Cloudflare's network is designed to absorb this kind of growth in DDoS threats. Every service on our network is protected by free, unmetered DDoS protection that runs at every one of our 330+ cities globally , backed by 500 Tbps of network capacity . Autonomy is the point: our systems detect and mitigate attacks without human intervention . And they need to, because as this quarter's distributions make clear, most attacks end long before a human analyst could see the alert, and the largest attacks still regularly exceed 1 Tbps at a cadence measured in hundreds per quarter. To help hosting providers, cloud computing platforms, and Internet service providers identify and take down the abusive IP addresses and accounts that launch these attacks, we leverage Cloudflare's unique vantage point on DDoS attacks to provide a free DDoS Botnet Threat Feed for Service Providers . Over 800 networks worldwide have signed up for this feed, and we've already seen great collaboration across the community to take down botnet nodes. For a continuously-updated view of attack trends across the Internet, visit Cloudflare Radar . items.title: CVE-2026-76418: Cisco Secure Firewall Zero-Day Exploited in SSL VPN Attacks
items.summary: Cisco has released security updates for CVE-2026-76418, a high-severity zero-day vulnerability affecting the Remote Access SSL VPN service in Cisco Secure Firewall Adaptive Security Appliance (ASA) and Secure Firewall Threat Defense (FTD) software. The flaw is being actively exploited in the wild and can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to force a vulnerable firewall to reload, causing a denial-of-service (DoS) condition and disrupting remote access. Cisco assigned the vulnerability a CVSS 3.1 score of 8.6. The flaw requires no authentication or user interaction and has low attack complexity. Its primary security consequence is loss of availability rather than confidentiality or integrity compromise. Cisco has not associated the vulnerability with remote code execution or confirmed data theft. The vulnerability is particularly important because edge security devices and VPN gateways are often directly exposed to the internet and provide critical access to corporate environments. Repeated exploitation could force affected appliances to restart and interrupt VPN connectivity for remote employees and administrators. Cisco disclosed the vulnerability on October 28, 2026, after its Product Security Incident Response Team (PSIRT) became aware of active exploitation during October. The issue was originally identified by Eric Fernald while resolving a Cisco Technical Assistance Center support case. For CVE-2026-76418 detection, security teams should prioritize monitoring internet-facing Cisco ASA and FTD appliances for unexpected reloads, repeated SSL VPN connection attempts, abnormal authentication activity, and availability disruptions affecting remote-access services. SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform enables security teams to strengthen visibility into vulnerability exploitation and suspicious behavior across SIEM, EDR, firewall, network, and identity telemetry. Click Explore Detections to access relevant detection content and threat hunting logic. To Detect CVE-2026-76418, defenders should combine firewall configuration assessment with VPN telemetry, device-reload events, network activity, and authentication logs to identify exploitation attempts and confirm exposure. Contact Sales CVE-2026-76418 analysis The vulnerability exists in the Remote Access SSL VPN functionality of Cisco Secure Firewall ASA and Secure FTD software. According to Cisco, the root cause involves logic errors that occur when secondary authentication is configured on a tunnel group. An unauthenticated attacker can send a specially crafted request while connecting to the SSL remote-access VPN service and trigger an unexpected device reload. Importantly, a successful VPN authentication is not required to reach the vulnerable processing path. This significantly increases the potential attack surface because an attacker only needs network access to the exposed SSL VPN service rather than valid VPN credentials. The details for CVE-2026-76418 indicate that three primary conditions must be present for a device to be exposed: The firewall must run a vulnerable Cisco Secure Firewall ASA or FTD release. The SSL Remote Access VPN login service must be reachable. Secondary authentication must be configured within an affected tunnel group. Cisco recommends administrators first determine whether SSL VPN functionality is enabled. On ASA systems, configurations containing webvpn with SSL VPN enabled on an interface require additional review. FTD administrators should inspect the deployed Remote Access VPN configuration through Secure Firewall Management Center or Device Manager. Administrators should then inspect tunnel groups for: secondary-authentication-server-group When tunnel-group-list enable is configured, every tunnel group should be examined, including DefaultWEBVPNGroup. Cisco specifically warns that checking only connection profiles displayed on the VPN login page is insufficient. Removing or disabling the tunnel-group list does not automatically eliminate exposure. If DefaultWEBVPNGroup still uses secondary authentication, the vulnerable path remains reachable. CVE-2026-76418 affects Cisco Secure Firewall ASA and Secure FTD deployments that satisfy these configuration conditions and run vulnerable software releases. Cisco has confirmed that the following products are not affected: Cloud-delivered Firewall Cloud-delivered Firewall Management Center Cisco Secure Access Secure Firewall Management Center Software The flaw is categorized as CWE-690, which relates to an unchecked return value leading to a NULL pointer dereference. Cisco’s CVSS vector reflects network accessibility, low attack complexity, no privileges required, no user interaction, and high availability impact. A successful attack does not provide the adversary with administrative access to the firewall based on the currently disclosed information. Instead, the appliance reloads unexpectedly, interrupting its availability. Depending on network architecture, repeated exploitation could have broader operational consequences. An affected firewall may provide remote connectivity for employees, administrators, partners, or third-party services. Interrupting that gateway can therefore interfere with business operations even without compromising data. Cisco has confirmed that attacks exploiting the vulnerability occurred during October 2026 but has not identified the threat actors responsible or disclosed victim information. CybersecurityNews likewise reports no confirmed connection to data theft or remote code execution. The issue should also be distinguished from other recently disclosed Cisco firewall vulnerabilities. It is separate from previously reported flaws affecting Cisco ASA and VPN infrastructure, with different technical causes and exploitation paths. At the time of writing, neither Cisco’s advisory nor the supplied reporting provides a public CVE-2026-76418 PoC containing reproducible exploit code. The absence of a public proof of concept does not reduce the urgency of remediation because Cisco has already confirmed real-world exploitation. Cisco has also not published campaign-specific CVE-2026-76418 IOCs, such as attacker IP addresses, domains, payload hashes, or named threat infrastructure. This means defenders should prioritize behavioral and configuration-based hunting rather than relying exclusively on static indicators. Potential investigation points include: Unexpected ASA or FTD reloads without an administrative or maintenance explanation Repeated connections to the public SSL VPN service immediately before a reload Clusters of abnormal remote-access VPN requests from external infrastructure Repeated availability disruptions affecting the VPN gateway Firewall uptime unexpectedly resetting Unusual authentication activity surrounding device restarts Repeated connections from the same or related IP ranges before service interruption Multiple unexplained appliance reloads over a short period Teams should also correlate firewall events with upstream network telemetry. Load balancers, edge routers, DDoS protection systems, IDS/IPS platforms, or external monitoring tools may retain evidence of connections that occurred immediately before the firewall became unavailable. Preserving this telemetry is especially important when the firewall itself is repeatedly restarted because some volatile diagnostic information may be lost. Organizations should additionally determine whether attackers attempted other activity before or after exploitation. Cisco currently characterizes the vulnerability as a denial-of-service flaw, so defenders should avoid automatically interpreting a device crash as evidence of full firewall compromise. However, an unexplained restart of an internet-facing security appliance still warrants investigation, particularly when exploitation has been confirmed in the wild. CVE-2026-76418 Mitigation Cisco has released fixed ASA and FTD software and strongly recommends upgrading because no complete workaround addresses the underlying vulnerability. The first fixed Cisco Secure Firewall ASA releases are: ASA release branch First fixed release 9.16 and earlier 9.16.4.104 9.18 9.18.4.96 9.20 9.20.4.50 9.22 9.22.3.200 9.23 9.23.1.48 9.24 9.24.1.27 / 9.24.10.1 For Secure FTD, Cisco lists: FTD release branch First fixed release 7.0 and earlier 7.0.11 7.2 7.2.13 7.4 7.4.9 7.6 7.6.7 7.7 7.7.14 10.0 10.0.3 10.1 10.1.1 Organizations should use Cisco’s Software Checker and compatibility documentation to determine the correct fixed release for their specific hardware and currently installed software branch. Although Cisco lists no workaround that fully addresses the vulnerability, it documents temporary configuration mitigations involving secondary authentication. The recommended CVE-2026-76418 mitigation depends on how tunnel groups are configured. If DefaultWEBVPNGroup does not use secondary authentication, administrators can disable the tunnel-group list using: no tunnel-group-list enable This prevents users from selecting a connection profile from a list and instead requires them to know the correct profile. If DefaultWEBVPNGroup does use secondary authentication, administrators can remove it using: no secondary-authentication-server-group However, Cisco warns that removing secondary authentication reduces the security posture of remote-access VPN authentication. Organizations should therefore carefully evaluate this temporary measure before deploying it. These changes should be considered temporary risk-reduction measures rather than replacements for patching. Because exploitation is already occurring, organizations should prioritize systems that are: Internet-facing Running vulnerable ASA or FTD releases Providing SSL remote-access VPN connectivity Using secondary authentication Supporting critical remote workforce or administrative connectivity Security teams should also verify whether high availability or failover architecture could reduce operational disruption while upgrades are performed. After applying updates, confirm the running software version and verify that the appliance has successfully returned to service. Administrators should review system logs covering the period before patching for unexplained reloads or other indications of exploitation. If suspicious activity is identified, preserve relevant: ASA or FTD system logs Remote-access VPN logs Authentication telemetry Firewall configuration history Upstream network flow data External monitoring data Identity provider logs associated with secondary authentication Because Cisco has disclosed only an availability impact, responders should distinguish confirmed evidence from speculation. An unexpected firewall restart does not by itself establish that an attacker obtained configuration files, credentials, or code execution. Nevertheless, organizations experiencing unexplained device reloads should review adjacent systems and authentication activity to ensure attackers were not simultaneously attempting other techniques. Administrators should also avoid delaying upgrades solely because no public exploit code is available. Active exploitation occurred before public disclosure, demonstrating that at least one attacker already possessed the capability to trigger the vulnerable behavior. Disclaimer: Detection content may not be available for every CVE. Check the SOC Prime Platform for current coverage. If relevant detections are not yet available, check again as new threat intelligence and detection content are continuously added. FAQ What is CVE-2026-76418 and how does it work? CVE-2026-76418 is a high-severity denial-of-service vulnerability in the Remote Access SSL VPN functionality of Cisco Secure Firewall ASA and Secure FTD software. The vulnerability results from logic errors triggered when secondary authentication is configured on an affected tunnel group. An unauthenticated remote attacker can send a crafted request to the SSL VPN service and cause the firewall to reload unexpectedly. A successful VPN login is not required to reach the vulnerable processing path. When was CVE-2026-76418 first discovered? Cisco publicly disclosed the vulnerability on October 28, 2026. The issue was identified by Eric Fernald while resolving a Cisco Technical Assistance Center support case. Cisco PSIRT became aware during October 2026 that attackers were already exploiting the vulnerability in real-world environments. What is the impact of CVE-2026-76418 on systems? Successful exploitation can force an affected Cisco ASA or FTD appliance to reload, causing a denial-of-service condition and interrupting firewall or remote-access VPN availability. Cisco assigns the vulnerability a CVSS score of 8.6 with high availability impact but no currently documented confidentiality or integrity impact. The vendor has not reported remote code execution or confirmed data theft resulting from the flaw. Can CVE-2026-76418 still affect me in 2026? Yes. The vulnerability is actively exploited and remains a risk for organizations running vulnerable Cisco ASA or FTD releases where the SSL remote-access VPN service is reachable and secondary authentication is configured in an affected tunnel group. Systems upgraded to Cisco’s fixed software releases are protected against the vulnerability described in the advisory. How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-76418? Upgrade Cisco Secure Firewall ASA or FTD software to the appropriate fixed release listed in Cisco’s security advisory. Administrators should also verify whether SSL remote-access VPN is enabled, inspect all relevant tunnel groups for secondary authentication, and review the DefaultWEBVPNGroup configuration. Where immediate patching is impossible, Cisco provides temporary mitigation options involving disabling the tunnel-group list or removing secondary authentication. Because these changes can affect functionality or reduce authentication security, they should be carefully evaluated and used only until the affected appliance can be upgraded.

Removing or disabling the tunnel-group list does not automatically eliminate exposure. If DefaultWEBVPNGroup still uses secondary authentication, the vulnerable path remains reachable.

CVE-2026-76418 affects Cisco Secure Firewall ASA and Secure FTD deployments that satisfy these configuration conditions and run vulnerable software releases.

Cisco has confirmed that the following products are not affected:

  • Cloud-delivered Firewall
  • Cloud-delivered Firewall Management Center
  • Cisco Secure Access
  • Secure Firewall Management Center Software

The flaw is categorized as CWE-690, which relates to an unchecked return value leading to a NULL pointer dereference. Cisco’s CVSS vector reflects network accessibility, low attack complexity, no privileges required, no user interaction, and high availability impact.

A successful attack does not provide the adversary with administrative access to the firewall based on the currently disclosed information. Instead, the appliance reloads unexpectedly, interrupting its availability.

Depending on network architecture, repeated exploitation could have broader operational consequences. An affected firewall may provide remote connectivity for employees, administrators, partners, or third-party services. Interrupting that gateway can therefore interfere with business operations even without compromising data.

Cisco has confirmed that attacks exploiting the vulnerability occurred during October 2026 but has not identified the threat actors responsible or disclosed victim information. CybersecurityNews likewise reports no confirmed connection to data theft or remote code execution.

The issue should also be distinguished from other recently disclosed Cisco firewall vulnerabilities. It is separate from previously reported flaws affecting Cisco ASA and VPN infrastructure, with different technical causes and exploitation paths.

At the time of writing, neither Cisco’s advisory nor the supplied reporting provides a public CVE-2026-76418 PoC containing reproducible exploit code. The absence of a public proof of concept does not reduce the urgency of remediation because Cisco has already confirmed real-world exploitation.

Cisco has also not published campaign-specific CVE-2026-76418 IOCs, such as attacker IP addresses, domains, payload hashes, or named threat infrastructure.

This means defenders should prioritize behavioral and configuration-based hunting rather than relying exclusively on static indicators.

Potential investigation points include:

  • Unexpected ASA or FTD reloads without an administrative or maintenance explanation
  • Repeated connections to the public SSL VPN service immediately before a reload
  • Clusters of abnormal remote-access VPN requests from external infrastructure
  • Repeated availability disruptions affecting the VPN gateway
  • Firewall uptime unexpectedly resetting
  • Unusual authentication activity surrounding device restarts
  • Repeated connections from the same or related IP ranges before service interruption
  • Multiple unexplained appliance reloads over a short period

Teams should also correlate firewall events with upstream network telemetry. Load balancers, edge routers, DDoS protection systems, IDS/IPS platforms, or external monitoring tools may retain evidence of connections that occurred immediately before the firewall became unavailable.

Preserving this telemetry is especially important when the firewall itself is repeatedly restarted because some volatile diagnostic information may be lost.

Organizations should additionally determine whether attackers attempted other activity before or after exploitation. Cisco currently characterizes the vulnerability as a denial-of-service flaw, so defenders should avoid automatically interpreting a device crash as evidence of full firewall compromise.

However, an unexplained restart of an internet-facing security appliance still warrants investigation, particularly when exploitation has been confirmed in the wild.

  • Internet-facing
  • Running vulnerable ASA or FTD releases
  • Providing SSL remote-access VPN connectivity
  • Using secondary authentication
  • Supporting critical remote workforce or administrative connectivity

  • Remote-access VPN logs
  • Authentication telemetry
  • Firewall configuration history
  • Upstream network flow data
  • External monitoring data
  • Identity provider logs associated with secondary authentication

Because Cisco has disclosed only an availability impact, responders should distinguish confirmed evidence from speculation. An unexpected firewall restart does not by itself establish that an attacker obtained configuration files, credentials, or code execution.

Nevertheless, organizations experiencing unexplained device reloads should review adjacent systems and authentication activity to ensure attackers were not simultaneously attempting other techniques.

Administrators should also avoid delaying upgrades solely because no public exploit code is available. Active exploitation occurred before public disclosure, demonstrating that at least one attacker already possessed the capability to trigger the vulnerable behavior.

FAQ

What is CVE-2026-76418 and how does it work?

CVE-2026-76418 is a high-severity denial-of-service vulnerability in the Remote Access SSL VPN functionality of Cisco Secure Firewall ASA and Secure FTD software. The vulnerability results from logic errors triggered when secondary authentication is configured on an affected tunnel group. An unauthenticated remote attacker can send a crafted request to the SSL VPN service and cause the firewall to reload unexpectedly. A successful VPN login is not required to reach the vulnerable processing path.

When was CVE-2026-76418 first discovered?

Cisco publicly disclosed the vulnerability on October 28, 2026. The issue was identified by Eric Fernald while resolving a Cisco Technical Assistance Center support case. Cisco PSIRT became aware during October 2026 that attackers were already exploiting the vulnerability in real-world environments.

What is the impact of CVE-2026-76418 on systems?

Successful exploitation can force an affected Cisco ASA or FTD appliance to reload, causing a denial-of-service condition and interrupting firewall or remote-access VPN availability. Cisco assigns the vulnerability a CVSS score of 8.6 with high availability impact but no currently documented confidentiality or integrity impact. The vendor has not reported remote code execution or confirmed data theft resulting from the flaw.

Can CVE-2026-76418 still affect me in 2026?

Yes. The vulnerability is actively exploited and remains a risk for organizations running vulnerable Cisco ASA or FTD releases where the SSL remote-access VPN service is reachable and secondary authentication is configured in an affected tunnel group. Systems upgraded to Cisco’s fixed software releases are protected against the vulnerability described in the advisory.

How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-76418?

Upgrade Cisco Secure Firewall ASA or FTD software to the appropriate fixed release listed in Cisco’s security advisory. Administrators should also verify whether SSL remote-access VPN is enabled, inspect all relevant tunnel groups for secondary authentication, and review the DefaultWEBVPNGroup configuration. Where immediate patching is impossible, Cisco provides temporary mitigation options involving disabling the tunnel-group list or removing secondary authentication. Because these changes can affect functionality or reduce authentication security, they should be carefully evaluated and used only until the affected appliance can be upgraded.

items.title: Chinese Hackers Use Secret Silent Train Network to Exploit Zero-Days Against U.S. Government and Defense
items.summary: China-linked Volt Typhoon hackers have used a covert network called Silent Train to hide zero-day attacks against U.S. government agencies, defense contractors and critical infrastructure. The network chains together compromised routers, connected devices and enterprise servers, helping operators reach sensitive systems while concealing where their activity begins. The investigation connects years of carefully targeted intrusions to attacks on centralized management platforms. These systems already hold trusted access to large networks, allowing attackers to steal credentials and reach customer environments without repeatedly breaking into individual machines. Researchers from Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs identified and tracked Silent Train over three years, issuing hundreds of victim notifications. Their October 28 report describes four confirmed zero-day campaigns and one likely campaign. Silent Train is an operational framework, not a single malware family; investigations also uncovered malicious in-memory webshells. Chinese Hackers Use Secret Silent Train Network First observed in November 2023, Silent Train grew as Volt Typhoon moved beyond its disrupted KV-botnet infrastructure. Earlier reporting on Volt Typhoon router exploitation documented the group’s use of compromised networking equipment as covert relays, but Lumen describes a more disposable and tightly controlled operating model. Sessions start on virtual private servers outside the United States, pass through compromised overseas devices, then enter U.S.-based infrastructure before reaching victims. Domestic exit points help traffic appear less suspicious and evade geographic restrictions. Some operations placed as many as six intermediary hops between the operator and target. High-level overview of the Silent Train chaining methodology (Source – Lumen) Lumen observed more than 27 device classes, including TP-Link routers, Netgear Orbi devices, Fortinet appliances and CyberPanel servers. Operators exploited exposed web interfaces and installed temporary SSH services, keys and configuration files. Chains could be assembled in under two minutes, while sessions averaged about four hours. Operators then removed their tools and dismantled the connections. Device roles remained consistent: Intelbras modems appeared as overseas relays, while Netgear Orbi devices served as U.S. hops. By early 2025, enterprise systems added longer-lived final connections that remained active for one to three months. Some sessions also used reverse tunnels instead of relying entirely on sequential SSH connections. Activity also followed a human work pattern. Most sessions occurred Monday through Friday, between 09:00 and 22:00 China Standard Time, with less activity overnight and on weekends. Individual sessions generally targeted one to five victims, often just one organization, underscoring the group’s selective use of the covert network. Management Platforms Give Attackers Wider Access The targets explain the value of this hidden infrastructure. Endpoint managers and software-defined wide-area network controllers provide device inventories, credentials and administrative functions. Previous coverage of exposed N-central management servers highlighted how weaknesses in one platform can threaten managed service providers and customers. Lumen linked Silent Train activity to exploitation of two previously undisclosed N-central vulnerabilities. Other campaigns targeted Versa Director, Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN and VeloCloud Orchestrator. Versa intrusions involved an in-memory JAR webshell that reduced evidence on disk. Cisco activity targeted trusted peering mechanisms, while VeloCloud became the third SD-WAN platform exploited through Silent Train. A separate Quest KACE campaign affected more than 30 victims, although limited logs prevented researchers from identifying the underlying flaw. Silent Train session chains (Source – Lumen) Lumen assessed the KACE zero-day link with moderate confidence, noting that activity declined after October 2025 security updates. That distinction matters: not every observed intrusion proves an unknown vulnerability was used, and the researchers could not determine the access method for every targeted product. The findings also extend earlier reporting on Cisco SD-WAN zero-day exploitation by showing Volt Typhoon using the affected control plane by late 2025 and continuing after disclosure in February 2026. Across campaigns, attackers harvested credentials, abused remote administration and file-transfer features, and sometimes altered or erased logs. Hawaii, California and Texas repeatedly emerged as targeting hotspots. Victims included telecommunications companies, satellite communications providers, universities with defense ties and essential service operators. Lumen considers the pattern consistent with positioning access inside networks supporting U.S. operations, particularly during Indo-Pacific crises, rather than evidence that disruption has already occurred. Defenders should restrict internet-facing management interfaces, prioritize vendor patches and review downstream trust relationships. Lumen also recommends exporting logs, extending retention and investigating unusual administrative activity, API requests, remote transfers and configuration changes. External logging is particularly important when attackers can erase evidence on the compromised platform. items.title: Highland Spring Appoints Acumen Cyber for 24/7 Cyber Protection
items.summary: Highland Spring Group , the business behind the UK’s number one bottled water brand, has selected Acumen Cyber to provide round-the-clock cybersecurity monitoring, threat detection and incident response. The partnership will see Glasgow-based Acumen Cyber deliver its managed security services to Highland Spring, helping the company strengthen its existing defences while giving its internal IT team more time to focus on strategic security improvements. Founded in 1979 and headquartered in Blackford, Perthshire, Highland Spring Group produces approximately 600 million litres of bottled water annually and employs around 500 people. The company has already invested significantly in its IT infrastructure and cybersecurity capabilities but recognised the need for additional specialist support to maintain continuous monitoring and respond to emerging threats. Strengthening Cybersecurity Across Operations Under the agreement, Acumen Cyber will provide 24/7 threat monitoring, investigation and response through its CREST-accredited Security Operations Centre (SOC) in Glasgow. The service combines security information and event management (SIEM), automation, threat intelligence and proactive threat hunting to help identify and respond to suspicious activity. Highland Spring’s IT team will work directly with UK-based security engineers, providing access to specialist expertise without having to manage round-the-clock security operations internally. The partnership is also intended to improve visibility of security risks and give Highland Spring’s team more capacity to strengthen infrastructure, address vulnerabilities and develop its longer-term cybersecurity strategy. Tracy Holbein, IT Manager at Highland Spring Group, said maintaining reliable operations was central to the decision. “Keeping our operations running reliably is essential to Highland Spring. This partnership will give us round-the-clock specialist support and more time for our own team to focus on preventing problems and strengthening our security.” She added: “Acumen stood out because of the rapport between our teams and their enthusiasm for working with us. That gave us confidence that we could build a close and productive partnership.” Engineer-Led Security Proves Deciding Factor Highland Spring selected Acumen Cyber following an extensive tender process, with the provider’s technical expertise, engineer-led approach and security platform playing an important role in the decision. The ability to work directly with the engineers responsible for delivering the service was particularly attractive, alongside Acumen’s CREST accreditation and fixed, predictable pricing. Another deciding factor was Acumen’s approach to continuously validating security controls against real-world attack techniques, helping customers understand how effectively their defences would perform during an actual incident. Mark Robertson, CEO of Acumen Cyber, said the partnership would focus on building a close working relationship with Highland Spring’s existing team. “Our role is to work as an extension of Highland Spring’s team, with named security engineers who understand the business and take responsibility for strengthening its defences.” He added: “That means continually improving protection as threats evolve and backing confidence with evidence. We continuously validate our detection capabilities against real-world attack techniques, using the findings to improve the security we deliver.” Supporting Long-Term Cyber Resilience The agreement reflects Highland Spring’s continued investment in cybersecurity as part of its wider business operations. For businesses with complex production, distribution and supply chain requirements, maintaining reliable systems and access to specialist security expertise is an important consideration. Acumen Cyber’s managed detection and response service is designed to provide continuous oversight while helping internal teams take a more proactive approach to identifying and reducing cyber risk. The partnership also builds on Acumen’s growing customer portfolio, with the company providing managed cybersecurity, continuous security testing, incident response, threat intelligence and strategic advisory services from its Glasgow headquarters.

items.summary: SOC Prime’s LogTotal now supports log exports from four major SIEM and EDR platforms: Google SecOps, CrowdStrike Falcon LogScale / Next-Gen SIEM, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (MDE), and Microsoft Sentinel. Each platform uses its own file formats, field names, and data model. LogTotal handles those differences automatically, so security teams can upload exports as they are and get the same depth of analysis from every source. Support for Splunk, IBM QRadar, and OpenSearch/Elasticsearch is coming next. Same event, four different descriptions Every platform records the same activity in its own way. A single process launch carries different field names depending on where it was exported from: What a detection looks for Google SecOps (UDM) Falcon LogScale / NG-SIEM Microsoft Defender for Endpoint Microsoft Sentinel (ASIM) Command line of the new process target.process.command_line CommandLine ProcessCommandLine TargetProcessCommandLine New process image target.process.file.full_path ImageFileName FolderPath + FileName TargetProcessName Parent or initiating process principal.process.file.full_path ParentBaseFileName InitiatingProcessFileName ActingProcessName The differences go beyond names: Different names for the same field. One concept, such as a command line, carries a different name on each platform. Different structure. UDM nests fields under principal and target, while MDE and Falcon use flat column names. Some values are split across fields, such as MDE’s FolderPath and FileName. Different naming within one platform. Next-Gen SIEM keeps native Falcon names for sensor telemetry and uses ECS-based CPS names for third-party data. Both can appear in a single export. Usually, analysts bridge these gaps by hand before a single rule can run. With LogTotal, these differences are not your problem. How LogTotal handles file formats LogTotal detects the file format for you. SOC Prime documents automatic detection of EVTX, CEF, JSON, and syslog , with no manual conversion. LogTotal accepts uploaded or pasted .log, .json, .jsonl, .evtx, .csv and .txt files of up to 3 GB or 3,000,000 events and processes up to 1.7 million events in under a minute. The platforms covered here differ most in how they package records: A single JSON array. LogScale’s JSON export wraps all events in one array. LogTotal reads each element as a separate event. CSV exports. Google SecOps, MDE advanced hunting, and Sentinel Logs export query results as CSV files, with each column header named after a field in that platform’s schema. You do not need to flatten nested JSON, rename columns, or reorder fields before upload. Sanitization then runs locally in your browser on the parsed events, so the same identifiers are tokenized consistently whichever format they arrived in. Users do not maintain mappings, write parsers, or choose a schema. This builds on mapping work SOC Prime already does for its detection content. SOC Prime’s platform support matrix lists rules for Google SecOps written against the UDM data schema, and Kusto queries for MDE and Sentinel written against their default schemas. LogTotal applies the same knowledge to exported files. After mapping, events from all four platforms go through the same pipeline: about 1,000,000 detection rules and 13,000 threat labels, correlated with Higher Order Sigma rules and agentic AI into attack chains mapped to MITRE ATT&CK. Use your platform’s standard export and upload the file as is. Mix sources in one investigation. Logs from different platforms are analyzed with the same rules and correlation, so findings are comparable. Keep your identifiers private. Rule coverage does not depend on which SIEM or EDR produced the file. How LogTotal handles file formats

LogTotal detects the file format for you. SOC Prime documents automatic detection of  EVTX, CEF, JSON, and syslog, with no manual conversion. The platforms covered here differ most in how they package records:

  • A single JSON array. LogScale’s JSON export wraps all events in one array. LogTotal reads each element as a separate event.

LogTotal takes care of format and schema differences for you. In practice:

  • Get the same depth on every platform. Rule coverage does not depend on which SIEM or EDR produced the file.

For best results, export the fields that carry detection value, such as process, command line, parent process, user, host, and network details, rather than a reduced summary view. Where a platform offers both, prefer the full event export over a column subset.

items.title: Hackers Claim Wagyu Crypto Platform Breach as Researchers Find Thousands of Monero Transaction Records
items.summary: Hackers have claimed a breach of cryptocurrency swap platform Wagyu.xyz, while researchers reviewing the purported leak found thousands of records connecting Monero transactions with public blockchain payments and IP addresses. The dataset contains 38,628 order records and 10,139 distinct IP addresses, covering activity between July 18 and October 26, 2026. Its origin and authenticity remain independently unverified. The findings highlight a privacy risk beyond cryptocurrency code: information held by services that move funds between blockchains. Unlike a wallet compromise, a transaction database leak can expose financial relationships without revealing private keys. The earlier Coinbase customer data breach similarly showed how exposed account information could create social-engineering risks without directly compromising customer funds. Researchers from Infostealers, Hudson Rock’s threat-intelligence publication, reported their findings on October 28. They noted that infostealer malware can expose credentials, browser activity and cryptocurrency information, but found no evidence that such malware caused this alleged incident or infected identified Wagyu customers. Hackers Claim Wagyu Crypto Platform Breach Ransomware-tracking services indexed WhiteArmor-associated listings naming Wagyu on October 27–28, including an entry titled “wagyu.xyz unfairness.” The accompanying claims focused on allegedly hidden swap fees and unfair coin-flip odds. However, a threat actor’s listing does not establish that ransomware was deployed, data was stolen, or financial misconduct occurred. Hudson Rock examined an order export and a separate IP-level activity summary. Researchers identified 8,137 orders naming native Monero receiving addresses, including 6,692 marked completed. Within the completed cross-chain subset, 4,580 records joined an incoming transaction hash, an XMR destination and a client IP address. That group included 1,011 Bitcoin-to-Monero orders. This matters because a swap provider must know where to deliver purchased coins. Its database may therefore connect a visible Bitcoin deposit with a Monero receiving address, timestamp, browser information and session identifier. These service-side records expose relationships that are not available through ordinary inspection of Monero’s blockchain. The wider risk involves combining separate sources of metadata. As reporting on stolen credentials fueling breaches explains, infostealer logs can contain browser sessions and wallet information. Such material could provide additional investigative context, although Hudson Rock did not report matching Wagyu records against infected users or stolen credentials. The records also show the reverse direction. Researchers found 11,317 native-XMR-input swap orders containing service deposit addresses and destinations for other assets. Among them, 9,187 completed records retained outgoing transaction hashes. These links can reveal a service’s public-chain payouts, but not which private Monero wallet originally supplied its deposits. Some transaction groups carried labels including “Poloniex Hacker,” “Theft” and “Tornado.Cash: 100 ETH.” Six completed withdrawals labeled “Poloniex Hacker” totaled $1,025,047 in recorded value. These are unverified database labels, not confirmed criminal attributions. Recorded amounts also do not establish stolen proceeds, and overlapping groups cannot be added into a reliable laundering total. Privacy Risks, Data Retention and User Protection The research does not demonstrate a weakness in Monero’s cryptography. Instead, it shows how information stored outside the blockchain can connect transaction requests and network activity. An IP address is not a verified identity: VPNs, Tor, shared networks and automated services can represent several users, while one person may use multiple addresses. Another concern involves 4,002 completed orders containing a populated userDeletedAt field. All retained an IP address and destination, while 3,180 also retained deposit transaction hashes. The field alone cannot establish what users deleted, whether backups were involved, or whether Wagyu breached any retention promise or legal obligation. If authentic, the records could support convincing refund scams, fake support messages or extortion attempts referencing real trades. Separate campaigns using fake crypto wallet screens demonstrate why users should never enter recovery phrases into unexpected prompts. Hudson Rock did not establish that anyone had exploited the alleged Wagyu leak this way. Users should verify notices through trusted channels and reject requests for private keys. Platforms should limit retention, restrict database access and explain how deletion affects logs and backups. items.title: Hackers Attack FreePBX Servers With Malware to Steal SIP Credentials for Phone Fraud
items.summary: Hackers targeting FreePBX phone servers have upgraded their malware to steal credentials that can keep phone fraud running even after an infected system is rebuilt. The INJ3CTOR3 operation now collects configuration files containing SIP trunk passwords, database credentials, management secrets, and mail relay logins, extending the damage beyond the compromised server. The change builds on an earlier campaign that placed unauthorized calls through victims’ own phone systems. Previously documented six-layer FreePBX persistence mechanisms helped the malware survive removal attempts, but stolen carrier credentials now give attackers another way to charge calls to a victim’s account. Researchers from Cyble Research & Intelligence Labs identified the updated malware while examining artifacts collected from the operation’s staging servers in September 2026. Their October 28 analysis describes an installer configured to upload 17 files repeatedly. Researchers recovered the upload commands but did not capture live exfiltration or establish a victim count. Hackers Attack FreePBX Servers With Malware The updated installer contains two encoded command groups, each directing configuration uploads to a separate staging server. Scheduled tasks run the installer every minute, repeatedly exposing secrets while the infection remains active. Changing passwords before removing the malware can therefore hand replacement credentials straight back to the attacker. The targeted files span FreePBX, Issabel, Elastix, Asterisk, and Postfix configurations. They include SIP and PJSIP authentication settings, Asterisk Manager Interface credentials, database passwords, and outbound mail authentication details. These files expose both calling services and supporting infrastructure. INJ3CTOR3 attack chain (Source – Cyble) SIP trunk credentials are particularly valuable because they authenticate a business’s connection to its telephone provider. Unless the carrier restricts access to approved IP addresses, stolen credentials can let attackers register from another machine and place calls without using the original PBX. Those calls may leave no records on the cleaned server. The operation retains its JOMANGY and ZenharR webshells, which provide remote commands and access to phone-system functions. Related FreePBX webshell exploitation activity previously demonstrated how attackers combine administrative access, backdoor accounts, and outbound calling capabilities to monetize compromised VoIP infrastructure. Cyble also found changes designed to weaken older detection rules. Webshell watermarks now vary between builds, and the password-gate hash has changed. The underlying persistence remains largely unchanged, including scheduled downloads, login triggers, protected backup files, and multiple webshell copies that can restore deleted components. Detection and Recovery Must Include Credential Rotation Investigators should not treat a normal-looking FreePBX dashboard as proof that a server is clean. In laboratory testing, Cyble created an Asterisk trunk directly in configuration files that carried calls without appearing in the FreePBX console. Researchers did not observe this campaign planting such a trunk. The malware also modifies web-server rewrite rules so requests containing encoded whitespace can reach a webshell without naming its file in access logs. k.php line 34, decoded into 17 file uploads (Source – Cyble) Meanwhile, the takeover script clears logs and command histories, reducing the evidence available for incident reconstruction. Recovery requires isolation, evidence preservation, and removal of persistence before rotation of exposed credentials. Earlier guidance covering FreePBX zero-day server compromises similarly recommends clean restoration and replacement of system, trunk, extension, and other account secrets rather than relying on patching alone. The panel’s Freepbx and Elastix buttons forge an admin session without a password (Source – Cyble) Administrators should coordinate with carriers to replace trunk secrets, preserve registration and billing records, restrict allowed source addresses, and set spending limits where available. Monitoring should cover unexpected registrations, premium-rate destinations, unusual call concurrency, and outbound configuration uploads. Cyble recommends rebuilding from a trusted image as the most reliable recovery option. items.title: Have an older iPhone or iPad? Apple has a security update for you
items.summary: Apple’s latest updates include a fix for a CoreGraphics bug that may have been exploited in targeted attacks. The fix is now available for older iPhones and iPads. Apple released security updates on October 26. Apple first fixed the flaw in iOS 26.7.1. Its latest updates also bring the fix to older devices that can’t run iOS 26, including the iPhone XS, iPhone XS Max, iPhone XR, and seventh-generation iPad. The iOS 18.7.11 update is a backport: it brings a fix from a newer software version to an older one. Here, Apple has made the fix available to older devices running iOS 18, so they can be protected without upgrading to an operating system they don’t support. Updates for your particular device The table below shows which updates are available and links to Apple’s security information for each one. You will see if there are updates available and be guided through installing them. Turn on Automatic Updates if you haven’t already—you’ll find it on the same screen. How to update your Mac To update macOS on any supported Mac, use the Software Update feature, which Apple designed to work consistently across all recent versions. Here are the steps: Click the Apple menu in the upper-left corner of your screen. Choose System Settings (or System Preferences on older versions). Select General in the sidebar, then click Software Update on the right. On older macOS, just look for Software Update directly. Your Mac will check for updates automatically. If updates are available, click Update Now (or Upgrade Now for major new versions) and follow the on-screen instructions. Before you upgrade to macOS Tahoe 26, please read these instructions . Enter your administrator password if prompted, then let your Mac finish the update (it might need to restart during this process). Keep your Mac plugged in and connected to the internet until the update is done. How to update your Safari browser Safari updates are included with macOS updates, so installing the latest version of macOS will also update Safari. To check manually: Open the Apple menu > System Settings > General > Software Update . If you see a Safari update listed separately, click Update Now to install it. Restart your device when prompted. Technical details The headline bug is CVE-2026-86950 , in CoreGraphics, Apple’s framework for drawing graphics, images and PDF content. It’s an out-of-bounds write flaw, where software writes data outside the memory set aside for it. The result is that “processing a maliciously crafted file may lead to arbitrary code execution.” Apple says it is aware of a report that the flaw may have been exploited in an “extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals” on versions of iOS before iOS 27. That wording indicates Apple believes the bug was used in real attacks against a limited group of users. Usually, journalists, activists and officials are the targets of this kind of attack. If you think you could be a target of highly sophisticated spyware, you should update, restart your phone, and consider applying Apple’s Lockdown Mode . Scammers know more about you than you think. items.title: GitHub Launches Copilot Fusion for Smarter and Cheaper AI Coding
items.summary: GitHub has launched Copilot Fusion, a system that automatically selects AI models for coding tasks , helping developers balance code quality, speed, and cost. Instead of choosing a model for every request, users select Fusion and let it decide how to handle the work. It is generally available in Visual Studio Code , Copilot CLI, the GitHub Copilot app , and JetBrains IDEs . Fusion is a model router and coordinator, not a new standalone model. It checks each request for reasoning, code generation, debugging, and tool needs, then chooses the models and steps needed to produce one final answer. It also considers system health and model availability when making those choices. Fusion uses three execution patterns. In Single mode, one model completes the task. Cascade starts with an efficient model, then uses a judge to inspect the draft and decide whether a stronger model should take over. Critique sends a draft to several models for independent reviews before the original model revises its answer using their combined feedback. These patterns can change within the same conversation. A simple request may use one model, while a difficult follow-up may trigger extra review. GitHub Launches Copilot Fusion GitHub says choosing a pattern adds little delay, although Cascade and Critique take longer because they involve additional model calls. Developers can follow progress and inspect which models contributed to the final response. Fusion Standard selects one model for everyday work. Fusion High supports larger, clearly defined tasks, including difficult bug fixes and changes across several files. Fusion Max targets work needing deeper reasoning. Fusion Fast serves speed-sensitive requests in Visual Studio Code inline chat and cannot be selected directly by users. According to GitHub’s documentation , paid Copilot users get a 30% discount on Fusion model costs through November 30, 2026, though High and Max can consume more AI credits than Standard. Fusion keeps the main conversation on the same model where possible to preserve cached tokens. Supporting models receive only the context they need. Model selection also follows subscription limits, administrator restrictions, data residency rules, and FedRAMP requirements. Supported local models can participate through Fusion Standard in a public preview. Extra AI review should not be mistaken for a security guarantee. Earlier reporting on GitHub Copilot prompt injection and the RoguePilot repository takeover flaw shows why untrusted project content remains a concern. Both issues were patched, and neither report establishes a vulnerability in Fusion. GitHub also warns that discarding a draft does not automatically undo file edits that draft already made. Developers must review workspace changes before committing them. Fusion works separately from subagents and doesn’t launch them, so its role is coordination rather than independent agent management. items.title: Microsoft Urges Entra ID Admins to Migrate from SMS and Voice Authentication to Passkeys
items.summary: Microsoft urged Entra ID administrators to migrate from SMS and voice authentication in Entra ID to passkeys before retirement begins on February 1, 2027, to reduce phishing risks and prevent sign-in disruptions. The reminder, published on October 27 under Message Center notice MC1528000, follows July announcements. Retirement covers Worldwide and Government Community Cloud environments and should finish in early February 2027. Administrators should not wait until the change reaches their tenant before preparing affected users. According to the Microsoft retirement notice , users with another registered sign-in method will use that method. They will not need to register a passkey to continue accessing their accounts. This makes checking existing authentication methods an important first step for administrators. Users whose only registered method is SMS or voice face a different process. Microsoft says they can use their existing method one final time to verify their identity. They must then register a passkey to keep signing in, making preparation important for organizations with many phone-dependent accounts. The announcement continues the shift covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s report on Microsoft making passkeys the default in Entra ID . However, this retirement applies specifically to Microsoft-provided phone authentication, not a complete ban on SMS and voice across Entra ID. Microsoft Urges Passkey Migration SMS and voice authentication remain exposed to phishing and SIM-swap attacks. Criminals can trick users into sharing verification codes or take control of an authentication phone number. Moving away from these methods reduces reliance on phone networks and codes that attackers can capture. As Microsoft’s passkey documentation explains, passkeys use public-key cryptography under FIDO standards. The user’s authenticator keeps the private key, while the service stores the public key. During sign-in, the authenticator signs a challenge after the user unlocks it with a PIN or biometric check. The credential works only with the website or application it was created for, helping prevent fake login pages from stealing reusable sign-in secrets. Cybersecuritynews.com’s coverage of UNC3944’s SIM-swap attacks shows why reducing dependence on phone-based verification matters. Administrators should identify users relying on SMS or voice, prioritize accounts without another registered method, and help users adopt passkeys or another supported option. Microsoft also asks organizations to notify employees and helpdesk teams about the deadline and the registration process. Organizations that need to retain phone authentication can configure a customer-managed telecom provider through the Microsoft Security Store. Microsoft’s provider guidance says configuration will be available starting October 30, 2026. Customers must review coverage, pricing, support, and contractual terms before deployment. Existing customer-managed providers are unaffected. Organizations that do not use Microsoft-provided SMS or voice need no action for this retirement. At the same time, affected customers must migrate or configure their provider before February 1. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

items.title: Strengthening API and MCP Security Through Token Risk Detection with Thales Imperva API Security
items.summary: Security teams can now investigate six token risks directly at the endpoint level, making it easier to prioritize findings and take action across their API estate. APIs depend on tokens to authenticate requests and control access. But weak signing algorithms, excessive token lifetimes, exposed credentials, and inadequate expiry enforcement can undermine that protection. Identifying these weaknesses is only the first step. Security teams also need to know which endpoints are affected, understand the associated risks, and give application owners clear guidance on remediation. The report found that sensitive data exposure in JWTs increased from 46.0% to 49.8% of token-risk detections year over year. It also found that the share of endpoints accepting expired tokens increased from 5.0% to 8.5% . Nearly 40% of endpoints with token risks had two or more authentication risks, showing why teams need to understand how weaknesses can overlap. Previously, security teams had to cross-reference the account-level report with API Inventory to locate affected endpoints. With the new enhancement, they can investigate these findings directly where they already manage API risks. What’s new in API Inventory? Token risks now appear as named values in the existing API Risks column, with three practical improvements. Filter by risk: Find endpoints associated with a specific issue, such as Expired Token Acceptance. Investigate at the endpoint level: Open an endpoint’s detail drawer to view the risk name, endpoint-specific description, and first and last detected dates. Access remediation guidance: Understand the finding and the recommended next steps without exposing the underlying tokens or credentials. The result is a more direct workflow: identify affected endpoints, investigate the issue, and coordinate remediation without translating account-level findings into a separate endpoint list. Six token risks. One place to investigate them. Thales’s Imperva API Security now surfaces six token and authentication risks directly in API Inventory. Token risk What it means Why it matters JWT Weak/Missing Algorithm A JWT uses a weak signing algorithm or lacks an appropriate algorithm. Depending on the implementation, token integrity may be undermined, potentially allowing forgery. JWT Excessive TTL A token remains valid longer than necessary. A stolen token may remain usable for an extended period. JWT Sensitive Data Exposure Sensitive information is present in JWT claims. JWT payloads are encoded, not inherently encrypted, and may be readable by anyone who obtains the token. Auth Details in Path Params Credentials or tokens are passed in URL path parameters. URLs may be captured in logs, proxies, and browser history. Expired Token Acceptance An API accepts a token after its expiry. Access may persist beyond the intended token lifetime. Basic Auth Token Exposure Reusable Basic Authentication credentials are exposed in requests. Captured credentials may be replayed until they are changed or invalidated. Together, these detections help teams investigate weaknesses in token integrity, lifetime, data confidentiality, credential handling, and expiry enforcement. From finding to fix The enhancement turns token risk findings into a more actionable endpoint-level workflow. Scope the issue. Filter API Inventory by a specific token risk to identify affected endpoints. Prioritize. Consider endpoint exposure, data sensitivity, and other risks associated with the same endpoint. Route for remediation. Share the endpoint-specific description and remediation guidance with the responsible application or engineering team. Verify. Review subsequent detection activity after the fix is deployed. First and last detected dates provide useful context, but teams should validate remediation against relevant traffic and other available evidence. Securing the authentication layer behind agentic AI As AI agents increasingly interact with business applications, internal services, and third-party systems, APIs remain a critical part of the security foundation. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) provides a standardized way for AI applications to connect with tools and external data sources, making secure authentication and credential handling important considerations for agentic workflows. This is where endpoint-level token risk detection becomes particularly relevant. Aligning with OWASP MCP01: Token Mismanagement & Secret Exposure OWASP’s MCP Top 10 Identifies MCP01: Token Mismanagement & Secret Exposure as a key security risk for MCP-enabled systems. Thales’s Imperva API Security’s six token risk detections align with authentication and credential-handling concerns relevant to MCP01: Weak or missing JWT algorithms can undermine token integrity. Excessive token lifetimes can extend the window in which a compromised token remains useful. Sensitive data in JWT claims can expose information if a token is obtained by an unauthorized party. Authentication details in URL paths can increase the risk of credential exposure through logs and intermediary systems. Acceptance of expired tokens can indicate that token expiry is not being enforced as intended. Exposed Basic Authentication credentials can create opportunities for credential reuse and replay. By surfacing these risks at the endpoint level, Imperva helps security teams investigate authentication weaknesses in APIs that support agentic workflows, where those endpoints are discovered and monitored by the platform. This is a focused contribution to MCP security, not a claim of comprehensive MCP protection. Token risk detection alone does not discover every MCP server, prevent prompt injection, enforce least-privilege permissions, or determine whether an agent’s actions are legitimate. It provides actionable insight into an important part of the security foundation on which these systems depend. As organizations adopt MCP and more autonomous workflows, understanding and remediating authentication weaknesses across their API estate becomes increasingly important. Make token risks easier to act on Security teams need more than a list of potential problems. They need to connect findings with the affected endpoints, the teams responsible, and the steps required to address them. With six token risks now surfaced directly in Thales’s Imperva API Security’s API Inventory, teams can filter findings, investigate endpoint-specific details, and access remediation guidance in one place. The goal is simple: make token risks easier to find, easier to understand, and easier to act on – one endpoint at a time. items.title: Would Your Employees Join a Fake Anthropic AI Preview?
items.summary: Since September 2026, threat actors have been sending emails that appear to be an invitation to a private Anthropic AI meeting, but are actually attempts to steal Google and Microsoft login credentials. Exclusive access to new AI technology is valuable to many organizations, which is why threat actors use it as a lure in their phishing emails. Risks to the organization from this campaign include threat actors compromising a sensitive account, accessing the account’s sensitive documents (e.g. proprietary marketing material), and using the compromised account as an initial vector to further infiltrate the organization. Employees must stay vigilant, as these phishing emails bypass current email security technologies due to the abuse of legitimate tools like URL shorteners and CAPTCHAs. Cofense Intelligence consolidates campaign data, including indicators of compromise (IOCs) such as malicious web addresses, phishing email content, and broader campaign context, into Active Threat Reports (ATRs), providing a comprehensive view of identified threats . ATRs contain the full infection chain from the initial phishing link to the final malware file or credential phishing resource. If one ATR IOC appears in the organization, cybersecurity professionals can read the ATR to understand the phishing attack’s impact and mitigations. Each ATR has been curated by a human analyst. This human-vetted intelligence provides context and the campaign information necessary to mitigate future phishing attacks. For this private Anthropic AI preview campaign, actionable intelligence can be found in ATRs 423868 , 423866 , and 423475 . Key Points The campaign contains a tantalizing, private offer to preview Anthropic AI technology, which may be enough for employees to click before inspecting the email. The video teleconference software GoTo Webinar, which is used to send legitimate meeting emails and is usually not blocked by email security technologies, was abused to send a threat actor’s URL instead. The URL shortener zpr[.]io, which turns long URLs into short links, has been abused to help these phishing emails bypass current email security technologies. CAPTCHAs, which are tests that confirm a real human is visiting the website, are similarly abused to prevent automated analysis. items.title: Hackers Chain PHP2Shell and Linux Kernel Exploits to Gain Root Access on 25 Servers
items.summary: Hackers combined PHP2Shell vulnerabilities with a Linux kernel exploit to gain root access on 25 servers across the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, including three systems in a US government-affiliated environment. Dream researchers uncovered the campaign’s files on October 25, revealing a path from exposed firewall management interfaces to internal Active Directory services. According to Dream’s investigation, the list includes custom exploits, target lists, attack logs, and roughly 40 post-compromise scripts. The affected firewall vendor has been notified, but its name and vulnerable software versions remain withheld for security reasons. PHP2Shell Exploit Chain Gained Root The attack paired PHP2Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 , with Fragnesia, a Linux kernel privilege escalation flaw tracked as CVE-2026-46300. Dream described the PHP2Shell code as a custom, nonpublic implementation tailored to the targeted firewall platform, rather than a copy of a known public exploit. PHP2Shell targeted PHP’s session.upload_progress feature within the firewall’s appweb management server. Through several stages, the attacker exhausted memory, leaked a memory address, and manipulated damaged memory structures to run commands as the restricted nobody user. Fragnesia then changed local authentication data, allowing the attacker to become root without a password. The full chain reportedly installed a root webshell in under 15 minutes. Although the final request connected both exploits, earlier requests prepared memory for execution. Cyber Security News previously covered PHP2Shell exploitation and the underlying flaws , providing context for this campaign. Using FOFA, the attacker identified about 19,000 internet-facing firewalls. Roughly 5,000 returned version information, and filtering by location and software version narrowed the list to 240 targets. The operation ultimately compromised 24 firewalls, leaving webshells on 22 without further recorded activity beyond that initial access. Two firewalls linked to a US government-affiliated organization received closer attention. Configuration data exposed internal systems and network details. After the first firewall crashed, the attacker compromised the second on October 24 and established a reverse SSH tunnel forwarding eight internal ports. Startup settings allowed the tunnel to survive reboots. At 11:35 UTC that day, the attacker used the same exploit chain through the tunnel against an internal firewall management server. This became the 25th compromised system and exposed centrally managed firewall settings and credentials. Attack Path From there, the attacker decrypted an LDAP service account password and listed Active Directory users and groups. Password spraying, backdoor account creation, and SAML signing key theft were attempted, but their success remains unknown. These limits matter when assessing Active Directory attack paths , rather than assuming full domain control. Recovered systems contained Claude Code and an aiscan setup configured with DeepSeek and Kimi. Chinese-language prompts and UTC+8 timestamps supported Dream’s assessment of possible Chinese links. However, researchers found no direct proof that AI wrote the exploits, established no named actor attribution, and did not describe the campaign as fully autonomous. Dream recommends deploying relevant patches under vendor guidance. The broader concern is stolen access: fixing the entry point does not establish whether credentials, webshells, or tunnels remain usable. Investigators must distinguish confirmed credential theft and directory access from the still unverified outcomes of the attacker’s later identity attacks. AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

items.title: Hackers Leak Records of 41,000 DHS Personnel, Exposing Undercover ICE Agents
items.summary: A leak of records covering more than 41,000 Department of Homeland Security employees and contractors has exposed contact details, work assignments, and links to sensitive operations, including undercover ICE work. Published on October 28, the archive reveals far more than a staff directory, offering a view of internal teams and reporting lines. Distributed Denial of Secrets released the collection under the name Icepick, crediting a group calling itself Department of Peace. Researcher and journalist Maia Arson Crimew built a search tool for the records. The nonprofit says the release supports public oversight, journalism, and requests for government records. DHS Data Leak According to reports, the records were last updated on August 19, 2026. They include names, email addresses, phone numbers, office locations, job titles, and supervisors. The files cover DHS and seven component agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Customs and Border Protection, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. CBP accounts for more than half of the records, while roughly 10,000 relate to ICE. About 6,200 cover US Citizenship and Immigration Services, and nearly 1,000 concern CISA. The collection represents about one seventh of the department’s workforce, not every DHS worker. The most sensitive details appear in more than 55,000 permission groups, which help control access to internal systems. WIRED identified 39 Homeland Security Investigations employees in groups containing “CUC,” a term government court records link to certified undercover operations. Other groups reference wiretaps, phone data analysis, and surveillance tools. DDoSecrets says the information came from an Okta single sign-on service used by DHS. However, Reuters could not confirm that claim . Okta said its systems were secure and that it had no evidence its data or systems had been compromised. No confirmed entry method has been disclosed. That distinction matters. A claimed theft from an organization’s identity service does not establish a breach of the identity provider itself. Separate reporting on attacks targeting Okta identity systems shows how criminals can target customer accounts through phone calls and false help desk requests. There is no confirmed link between those methods and this incident. Reuters could not verify the entire archive. It matched details for six employees against other records and confirmed phone numbers and other information by calling three workers. Some entries matched public profiles, while others revealed internal structures or previously undisclosed operations. Names become more useful to attackers when paired with supervisors, duties, and phone numbers. Recorded Future expert Alexander Leslie told WIRED that such information could help adversaries identify vulnerable staff, build convincing impersonation attempts, or threaten investigations. Group membership, however, should not automatically be treated as proof of a person’s current assignment. Previous Okta support impersonation campaigns show why exposed contact details matter. Attackers have used fake support messages and login pages to steal account information and authentication codes. The DHS records could provide material for similarly tailored approaches. The disclosure follows ShinyHunters’ September claim of stealing FBI personnel data and an October lawsuit over a Defense Department breach affecting millions. These are separate incidents, with no established common cause. AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?
